overview: The Susquehannock were an Iroquoian-speaking regional power. This card also covers the map’s Susquehanna label, dated 1530 to 1650. Its earlier 1492 to 1500 outline is overbroad: communities around 1500 lay farther up the river than the later major towns. These shapes do not establish fixed borders or a people’s lifespan.

periods.title: Upper river communities
periods.summary: Early communities preceded the large lower-valley towns.

periods.title: Trade and fortified towns
periods.summary: The Susquehannock became important partners and rivals in colonial trade and diplomacy.

periods.title: Dispersal and later communities
periods.summary: Survivors rebuilt communities after war; later records preserve descendants beyond the Conestoga massacre.

sections.title: A trading power with changing towns

items.text: Archaeological and historical research places communities ancestral to the later Susquehannock along the North Branch around 1500. They subsequently moved south toward Lancaster County. Scholars debate the balance between pressure from neighboring peoples and opportunities for trade in explaining that movement.

Footpaths connected the Susquehanna with European trading settlements near the Delaware and Chesapeake. Heavy dugout canoes served fishing, cargo carrying and crossings, but were difficult to haul over land. A trading journey could therefore involve a well-known walking route as much as a river voyage.

The 1652 Treaty of Friendship with Maryland gave the Susquehannock a colonial ally and greater access to southern food resources. It eased conflict on one front while rivalry with the Haudenosaunee continued to the north. Diplomacy affected the practical questions of where families could safely hunt, fish and travel.

By 1675, war and disease had badly weakened Susquehannock power. A group moved to a fort near the Potomac, where Maryland and Virginia forces besieged them. Five chiefs who came out to negotiate were killed. Survivors escaped, and some later returned to the Susquehanna Valley.

Large towns contained longhouses where several related families lived together, with relationships traced through the female line. Around the stockade lay fields of corn, beans and squash. Shared buildings and nearby farmland made household life part of a densely connected community.

At Schultz, a lower-valley town occupied approximately from 1575 to 1600, rubbish and burned deposits preserve traces of a varied diet. Crops were supplemented with deer, bear, elk, fish, wild plants and nuts. Dinner depended on cultivated fields, woods and river together.

Some Susquehannock pots have tall decorated collars with small human faces. The Heritage Area describes these vessels as useful for meals or storing personal objects, including needles and fishhooks. A carefully decorated container could still have an ordinary household job; useful things did not have to look plain.

At Ibaugh, a village and cemetery dated about 1600 to 1625, clusters of tiny glass beads appear to have been sewn onto clothing. Children’s burials contained more beads than adult burials in the excavated sample. These patterns reveal care in dress and burial, without providing a simple measurement of family wealth.

At the mid-seventeenth-century Strickler site, contact with metal preserved pieces of trade cloth and blankets that would normally decay. The same collections contain cooking kettles and both Native-made and imported pipes. A lucky survival of fragile fabric can add clothing and bedding to an archaeological story dominated by hard objects.

Winter also offered time for company and teaching. Heritage researcher Paul Nevin suggests that longhouse evenings included stories and games, drawing on archaeology and related Iroquoian traditions. This is an informed reconstruction of social life, rather than a surviving timetable for one Susquehannock family.

A study published in 2020 examined the remains of 102 people from Pennsylvania and Maryland sites. Researchers found fewer signs of childhood growth disruption and some dental problems in the later group, interpreting this as possible improvement after the 1652 treaty. Political security can leave traces in health, although such samples require careful comparison.

A short written Susquehannock example is “Generoo,” glossed “Good friend” in a vocabulary published by Thomas Campanius Holm in 1702 and reproduced by linguist Marianne Mithun. The material came from earlier missionary recording. It preserves a historical transcription in European letters, not proof that Susquehannock communities already used an alphabet in 1492.

Excavations at later Conestoga Town reveal smaller, cabin-like homes with more space between them, rather than the earlier packed longhouse settlement. The community included people of different backgrounds. Changes in buildings and neighborhood layout record rebuilding after displacement, not simply an unchanged old town with a new name.

In 1763, the Paxton Boys attacked Conestoga residents. People who survived the first attack were taken to Lancaster for protection, but the attackers killed them there too. The massacre destroyed that community. It must be distinguished from a claim that all people with Susquehannock ancestry were present or killed.

An 1845 claim found in Lancaster’s legal records was made by three people living among the Oneida who identified Susquehannock ancestry and sought compensation for lost land. This later document helps challenge older accounts that treated the Conestoga massacre as the disappearance of every descendant.

ending.text: The large independent towns lost their power during seventeenth-century warfare and dispersal. Conestoga suffered massacre in 1763, but surviving families elsewhere prevent treating that event as the extinction of all Susquehannock descent.
